title: KPI Calculation Pipeline (SQL-equivalent in pandas)
text:
Each function below mirrors a BigQuery SQL view from the framework. The same logic, column names, threshold rules, and performance status labels are used. In production, these would be CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW statements executed in BigQuery.
Prerequisite: df_clean comes from Section 3.2 (facility DQ report cell). If you only skipped that cell, the first KPI code cell recomputes df_clean from df_raw_assessed automatically.


This section calculates the first Key Performance Indicator (KPI): the 30-day hospital readmission rate for each facility by month.

It replicates the logic of the BigQuery SQL view oaltc_kpi.readmission_rate_monthly, but executes it using pandas.
For each facility and month, it counts how many discharged residents were readmitted within 30 days (readmitted_30d).
The rate is then calculated as the percentage of readmissions out of total discharges for that period.
Facilities are categorized based on their rates:

“ALERT” if the rate is above 22%,
“WARNING” if between 18–22%,
“ON TARGET” if 18% or below.

The resulting table is used for performance management and reporting.

Example aggregation counts (performance_status):
KPI: 30-Day Readmission Rate — 650 facility-month records
performance_status
ON TARGET    321
ALERT        201
WARNING      128



This section introduces the second key performance indicator (KPI) used in the OALTC framework: the Staff Turnover Rate, calculated on a quarterly basis. The Staff Turnover Rate measures the frequency at which staff members (such as nurses and support staff) leave their positions within a nursing home or care facility during a given quarter. This metric is important for monitoring workforce stability, as high turnover rates can negatively impact the continuity and quality of care.
In the notebook, data from workforce submissions is aggregated per facility and quarter to calculate both the total number of staff separations and the average number of staff present. The turnover rate is then computed as the percentage of separations relative to the average headcount.
Facilities are categorized based on their turnover rates:

“ALERT” if the turnover rate is above 50%
“WARNING” if it is between 38% and 50%
“ON TARGET” if it is 38% or below

This KPI helps identify facilities with potential staffing instability and informs workforce management strategies.
Example:
KPI: Staff Turnover Rate — 293 facility-quarter records
performance_status
ON TARGET    293



This section introduces the third key performance indicator (KPI) in the OALTC framework: Pressure Ulcer Incidence Rate. This metric tracks the rate of new pressure ulcers among residents, typically expressed per 1,000 resident days, to gauge the quality of care and preventive practices in facilities. A high incidence rate may indicate gaps in care processes, while lower rates reflect effective prevention and monitoring efforts. The notebook calculates this KPI on a quarterly basis for each facility.
Example:
KPI: Pressure Ulcer Rate — 250 facility-quarter records
performance_status
ON TARGET    158
ALERT         92



This section introduces the fourth key performance indicator (KPI) in the OALTC framework: Timely Complaint Investigation Rate. This metric measures the percentage of complaints that are investigated and resolved within a specified number of days (e.g., 10 days), serving as an indicator of regulatory compliance and responsiveness to resident concerns. Higher rates reflect prompt resolution and regulatory alignment, while lower rates may highlight areas needing process improvements or additional oversight. The notebook calculates this KPI on a monthly basis for each facility.
Example:
KPI: Complaint Timeliness — 412 facility-month records
performance_status
ON TARGET    268
ALERT        129
WARNING       15



This section introduces the fifth key performance indicator (KPI) in the OALTC framework: the Outcome Disparity Index. The Disparity Index measures health equity by quantifying the gap in 30-day hospital readmission rates between racial and ethnic groups within each region and time period. A lower index indicates more equitable outcomes, while a higher index signals greater disparity. This metric helps identify regions and time periods where disparities in health outcomes exist, enabling targeted interventions to address inequities.
The notebook computes the index by comparing readmission rates among different groups and defines performance thresholds to flag areas of significant disparity.

In this step, the code builds a consolidated “KPI Data Mart,” which brings together key performance indicator values for each facility into a single, analytics-ready dataframe.
This mart aggregates the latest available snapshots for:

Readmission rates
Staff turnover rates
Complaint investigation timeliness
Facility characteristics (e.g., bed count, ownership)

It also computes a unified “composite risk score” (0–100) for each facility based on those KPIs, and assigns an overall performance status (ALERT, WARNING, ON TARGET). This summary data mart is designed to drive dashboards and decision support.
If complaint KPIs were not run in the kernel, the notebook warns and leaves timeliness fields as NaN until 3.3d is executed:

overall_status
ON TARGET    26
ALERT        14

The table above displays a preview of the executive-level “KPI Data Mart”, which summarizes Tier 1 KPI performance for each facility for the most recent available period.
Key columns include:

facility_id, facility_name, region: Facility identifiers and regional grouping.
readmission_rate_pct, turnover_rate_pct, timeliness_rate_pct: Each facility’s latest 30-day readmission, workforce turnover, and complaint timeliness rates.
readmit_status, turnover_status, complaint_status: Highlight which metrics triggered ALERT or WARNING statuses, based on defined thresholds.
licensed_beds, facility_type, ownership: Facility characteristics.
composite_risk_score: Combined, weighted KPI risk score (higher = more concern).
overall_status: Summary flag, set to ALERT if any single KPI is in alert, otherwise WARNING or ON TARGET.

This mart enables rapid triage and prioritization by spotlighting facilities at greatest risk based on latest quality, workforce, and regulatory indicators.

title: Requirements Gathering
text:
Within the OALTC Data Analyst 3 role, requirements gathering involves visiting program offices to identify questions staff currently cannot answer about their programs. These needs are then translated into concrete data and analytical specifications.


Without a thorough requirements gathering process, there is a significant risk of developing solutions that do not address stakeholder needs. A common failure occurs when, for example, an analyst spends weeks building a dashboard tracking facility inspection completion rates, only to later discover that the program manager actually required data on complaint resolution times, not inspection rates, and already had access to the inspection data elsewhere.
Requirements gathering addresses this problem by ensuring alignment between stakeholder needs, available data, and feasible solutions.



Every requirements gathering process, whether formal or informal, is aimed at answering the following:

What decision is the analysis intended to support? The relevant question is not simply about data, but about the action that the data will inform. For example, a program may need to decide which facilities should be prioritized for unannounced inspections in the upcoming quarter.
What does success look like? This refers to how success will be measured. For example, the goal may be to flag the top 10% of highest-risk facilities two months before a deficiency citation occurs.
What data is already available? This involves taking inventory of current systems, spreadsheets, reports, and any existing data sources. It is necessary to clarify who owns each data source and how frequently they are updated.
What is missing or broken? This step identifies gaps, such as missing fields, inconsistent definitions, or data that exists only on paper.
Who needs to see the output, and in what form? Different stakeholders have different needs: a Commissioner may prefer a one-page summary; a program manager might need a filterable table; a surveyor could require a facility-level flag. The same underlying data may require multiple presentations.




In the OALTC setting, requirements gathering follows these stages:


The analyst meets with program offices, such as Nursing Home, Home Care, Adult Day Services, and Assisted Living, to ask structured questions, for example: - Describe the current reporting process: outputs, audiences, and frequency - Identify which questions consistently arise in leadership meetings that present data cannot answer - Explore what information would ideally appear on a dashboard - Determine which decisions are delayed due to unavailable data - Discover what data is routinely collected but seldom used
All responses are documented. No commitments are made at this stage; the focus remains on active listening.



Simultaneously, the available data across BigQuery, ITS-managed applications, and other sources (spreadsheets, Access databases, manual logs) is audited. The process includes mapping existing tables, fields, data completeness, and update frequency, identifying which needs can be met with current data, and flagging requirements for new data feeds.



Not every stakeholder request can be implemented right away. Program leadership works with analysts to rank use cases based on impact (importance to decision-making) and feasibility (difficulty given data availability). High-impact and high-feasibility items receive top priority. An example prioritization:

Every approved use case is documented to cover: - Business requirement: what the stakeholder needs, stated plainly - Functional requirement: what the system is required to do (e.g., calculation of 30-day readmission rates at the facility level, and at what frequency) - Data requirement: specific tables, fields, filters, and business rules - Output requirement: definition of the audience, format, frequency, and level of detail required - Acceptance criteria: conditions under which the stakeholder will verify the solution is correct



The requirements document is reviewed and signed by the program office before any development begins. This provides mutual assurance about scope and deliverables.




Stakeholders may describe what they want, not what they actually need. For instance, requesting “all the data in one place” may mask a need for a concise weekly summary. Analysts should probe by asking, “What would you do differently if you had that?”
Requirements creep is another risk. New ideas can emerge in every conversation, causing scope to expand unless new ideas are managed in a backlog for later assessment.
Assumptions based on prior domain knowledge can be dangerous, as each program office may operate with different workflows and definitions. Analysts are advised never to assume but always to ask and document.
Technical jargon can exclude stakeholders. For example, instead of asking about ETL requirements, it is better to ask, “How does the data get from the facility to your desk today, and where does it break?”

Pitfall
Recommended mitigation

Written agreement must be obtained from both parties prior to any development, in order to maintain agreed scope.

Prepared by: Zia U. Ahmed, Ph.D. • May 2026
This document presents a comprehensive, end-to-end framework for defining, tracking, and reporting Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for OALTC-licensed programs. The framework is structured around five interconnected components: (1) strategic alignment and KPI governance, (2) KPI taxonomy and definition standards, (3) data infrastructure and pipeline architecture using Google BigQuery, (4) dashboard and reporting design, and (5) continuous improvement and stakeholder engagement. Together, these components equip the Bureau of Data Analytics and Automation to deliver timely, accurate, and actionable performance intelligence to OALTC program leaders, senior DOH leadership, and external stakeholders.
The framework is designed to be scalable across all OALTC program types — including nursing homes, assisted living programs, adult day services, home care agencies, and continuing care retirement communities — and is aligned with OALTC’s core strategic priorities of quality of care, regulatory compliance, operational efficiency, workforce stability, and health equity.




All KPIs in this framework are anchored to OALTC’s five core strategic priorities. Every metric must trace directly to at least one of these pillars:

1
Quality of Care
Resident/client outcomes, safety events, care standard adherence across licensed facilities
Program Directors, DOH Leadership


2

Inspection outcomes, deficiency rates, complaint resolution timeliness, enforcement actions
Surveyors, Legal, Leadership


3
Operational Efficiency
Data submission compliance, processing times, workflow automation, cost-per-case metrics
Bureau Chiefs, IT, Finance


4

Staff turnover rates, vacancy rates, training completion across regulated providers
Program Managers, Workforce Unit


5
Health Equity
Disparity metrics by race, ethnicity, geography, payer type; access and outcome gaps across population groups
Health Equity Team, DOH Commissioner






Robust KPI governance ensures accountability, consistency, and continuous relevance of all metrics. The following three-tier governance model is recommended:

Tier 1 — Strategic KPIs: Reviewed by DOH senior leadership and OALTC Director on a quarterly basis. These are high-level outcome indicators tied directly to OALTC’s mission and reported in public-facing documents.
Tier 2 — Operational KPIs: Reviewed by Bureau Chiefs and Program Managers monthly. These track day-to-day program performance and early warning signals.
Tier 3 — Analytical KPIs: Reviewed by the Data Analytics team weekly. These are granular metrics used to monitor data quality, pipeline health, and emerging trends before they escalate.
Each KPI is assigned a designated Data Owner (the program office responsible for the metric), a Data Steward (the analytics team member responsible for the data feed), and a Business Reviewer (the stakeholder who interprets and acts on the metric).
A KPI Registry — maintained in a version-controlled document linked to the BigQuery metadata catalog — serves as the single source of truth for all active metrics, their definitions, data sources, owners, and update schedules.







KPIs are organized into four functional categories that span the full program performance lifecycle:

Outcome KPIs: Measure the end results of care and services (e.g., hospitalization rates, resident satisfaction scores, deficiency citation counts).
Process KPIs: Measure whether program activities are being executed as intended (e.g., timely completion of care assessments, inspection cycle adherence).
Capacity KPIs: Measure resources and infrastructure (e.g., licensed bed occupancy, staff-to-resident ratios, data system uptime).
Equity KPIs: Measure disparity and access gaps across demographic and geographic subgroups (e.g., outcome differentials by race/ethnicity or rural vs. urban location).




Every KPI must be formally defined using the following standardized template before it enters the tracking system. Consistency in definition prevents misinterpretation and ensures comparability over time.

The KPI tracking system is built on Google BigQuery as the central data warehouse. The architecture follows a four-layer pipeline model: Ingestion → Storage → Transformation → Presentation.

Layer 1 — Ingestion: Raw data flows into BigQuery from OALTC-licensed program submissions, ITS-managed applications, Medicaid claims, MDS feeds, and survey system exports. Each data feed is assigned a schema, ingestion schedule, and validation ruleset.
Layer 2 — Raw Storage (Data Lake): Unprocessed source data is stored in partitioned BigQuery tables by program, date, and source system. All raw records are retained for auditability and reprocessing.
Layer 3 — Transformation (Data Mart): SQL-based ETL pipelines transform raw data into clean, analysis-ready tables. KPI calculations, denominator logic, and exclusion rules are encoded here using version-controlled SQL scripts or dbt models.
Layer 4 — Presentation: Transformed KPI tables power dashboards (Looker Studio or Tableau), automated reports, and self-service query interfaces for OALTC program staff.




Data quality is enforced at each pipeline stage using the following six-dimension framework:









Dimension
Definition
Validation Rule (Example)
Action if Failed


Completeness
All required fields are populated
Null rate < 2% for facility_id, report_date, and outcome fields
Flag record; alert Data Steward; exclude from KPI calc until resolved


Validity
Values fall within defined ranges and formats
Readmission rate between 0–100%; date format = YYYY-MM-DD
Reject record; log error; notify submitter


Timeliness
Data arrives within the expected submission window
Monthly feeds ingested by the 10th of the following month
Trigger escalation alert; mark period as provisional


Consistency
Values are consistent across linked tables and time periods
Facility bed count in submissions matches licensed capacity in registry
Flag discrepancy; hold for reconciliation


Accuracy
Values reflect real-world program activity
Outlier detection: z-score > 3 triggers manual review
Queue for analyst review; annotate in dashboard


Uniqueness
No duplicate records in the analysis dataset
Composite key (facility_id + resident_id + event_date) must be unique
De-duplicate; log count of removed records






Each KPI is computed via a standardized SQL view in BigQuery. Below is the generalized template:




CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW oaltc_kpi.readmission_rate_monthly AS
SELECT
facility_id,
facility_name,
report_year,
report_month,
COUNT(CASE WHEN readmitted_30d = TRUE THEN 1 END) AS numerator,
COUNT(*) AS denominator,
ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNT(CASE WHEN readmitted_30d = TRUE THEN 1 END),
COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS readmission_rate_pct,
CASE
WHEN SAFE_DIVIDE(…) * 100 > 20 THEN ‘ALERT’
WHEN SAFE_DIVIDE(…) * 100 > 15 THEN ‘WARNING’
ELSE ‘ON TARGET’
END AS performance_status
FROM oaltc_raw.nh_discharge_events
WHERE data_quality_flag = ‘PASS’
AND discharge_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 13 MONTH)
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4;

The following reporting schedule ensures stakeholders receive the right information at the right time:

Daily: Automated data quality alerts sent to Data Stewards for any pipeline failures, validation errors, or submission gaps. No manual action unless thresholds are breached.
Weekly: Program Performance Monitor refreshed and shared with Bureau Chiefs. Includes a summary of KPIs in ALERT or WARNING status and any emerging trends.
Monthly: Full KPI report package distributed to OALTC Program Directors. Includes trend analysis, month-over-month comparisons, facility-level rankings, and commentary on outliers.
Quarterly: Strategic Scorecard presented to DOH senior leadership. Includes progress toward annual targets, equity gap analysis, and narrative summary for each strategic pillar.
Annual: Year-end performance review document. Includes baseline resets, target revisions, lessons learned, and proposed additions or retirements to the KPI Registry.




A tiered alert system ensures that performance signals translate into timely action:










Alert Level
Trigger Condition
Notification
Required Action
Timeline


⚠️ WARNING
KPI exceeds 10% above target for one reporting period
Automated email to Program Manager and Data Steward
Analyst investigates root cause; documents findings in KPI log
Within 5 business days


🔴 ALERT
KPI exceeds warning threshold for two consecutive periods OR single-period breach is severe
Automated alert to Bureau Chief and Program Director; included in weekly summary
Bureau Chief reviews; corrective action plan initiated; escalated to OALTC Director if unresolved
Within 2 business days


✅ ON TARGET
KPI within or better than target range
Reflected in dashboard; highlighted in monthly report
No action required; document and share as best practice if sustained ≥ 3 months
Monthly review









While standard KPI tracking captures what has happened, the Bureau of Data Analytics and Automation can deliver significantly greater value by layering predictive and explanatory analytics on top of the core KPI framework. This transforms the system from a rearview mirror into an early-warning and decision-support tool.




Ensemble machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost) can be trained on historical KPI trends to predict which facilities are at elevated risk of deteriorating performance in the next 30–90 days — enabling proactive intervention before a deficiency occurs.
Time-series forecasting (ARIMA, Prophet, LSTM) can project KPI trajectories under different intervention scenarios, supporting resource allocation planning.
Risk stratification models can flag facilities for prioritized oversight based on a composite risk score combining multiple KPIs, complaint history, and staffing data.





SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values can identify which factors — staffing levels, ownership type, payer mix, geographic context — are the primary drivers of KPI variation across facilities.
Geographically Weighted models can reveal whether the relationship between staffing and outcomes differs by region, enabling targeted policy responses rather than one-size-fits-all interventions.





Stratified KPI analysis by race, ethnicity, payer type, and geography quantifies disparity gaps and tracks progress toward equity goals over time.
Spatial clustering analysis (Moran’s I, LISA) can identify geographic hotspots of poor performance, directing inspection and support resources to underserved areas.







New KPIs are developed through a structured five-step process to ensure relevance, feasibility, and buy-in:









Step
Activity
Description
Responsible Party


1
Use Case Discovery
Structured interviews and workshops with program offices to identify analytical needs and performance questions they cannot currently answer
Data Analyst 3 + Program Managers


2
Data Feasibility Assessment
Evaluate whether required data exists in BigQuery, the expected data quality, and any gaps that require new data feeds or collection instruments
Data Steward + IT


3
KPI Definition & Review
Draft formal KPI definition using the standard template; review with program office for accuracy and business relevance
Data Analyst 3 + Data Owner


4
Pilot & Baseline
Calculate the KPI for at least 12 months of historical data to establish baseline; review with stakeholders before setting targets
Data Analyst 3


5
Register & Deploy
Add approved KPI to the KPI Registry, build the BigQuery view, connect to dashboard, and train program staff on interpretation
Data Steward + Data Analyst 3






The KPI portfolio is reviewed annually to ensure ongoing relevance:

Retire KPIs that are no longer aligned with strategic priorities or where the underlying program has changed.
Revise targets based on actual performance trends, new benchmarks from CMS or peer states, and updated strategic goals.
Add new KPIs identified through the use-case discovery process or driven by new data feeds coming online.
Assess data quality trends for each KPI and invest in data improvement efforts for metrics showing persistent quality issues.




A key goal is to build data literacy within OALTC program offices so that staff can independently explore KPI data without relying solely on the analytics team for every question:

Develop user guides and short training modules for each dashboard, tailored to the non-technical program officer.
Create a curated library of pre-built BigQuery queries that program staff can run directly for common ad-hoc questions.
Host quarterly ‘Data Office Hours’ sessions where program staff can bring analytical questions and learn best practices for interpreting KPI trends.





The framework is implemented in four phases over 12 months:









Phase
Timeline
Key Activities
Deliverables


Phase 1 Foundation
Months 1–3
Stakeholder interviews; data inventory; KPI Registry v1.0 (15–20 priority KPIs); BigQuery data quality audit; establish governance structure
KPI Registry; Governance Charter; Data Quality Baseline Report


Phase 2 Core Build
Months 4–6
Build BigQuery transformation pipelines for Priority KPIs; deploy Operational Dashboard and Program Performance Monitor; set baselines and initial targets
Two live dashboards; 20 active KPI SQL views; Target-Setting Report


Phase 3 Expansion
Months 7–9
Add equity KPI layer; build Executive Scorecard; deploy predictive risk model for facility oversight prioritization; launch staff training program
Executive Scorecard; Equity KPI Module; Risk Stratification Model


Phase 4 Maturity
Months 10–12
Annual KPI review; refine alert thresholds based on operational experience; expand self-service analytics; document full framework for handover and sustainability
Updated KPI Registry; Year-1 Performance Report; Sustainability Plan



This framework provides OALTC with a scalable, evidence-based foundation for performance management. By combining rigorous KPI governance, a robust BigQuery data architecture, tiered dashboards, and predictive analytics, the Bureau of Data Analytics and Automation can move from reactive reporting to proactive program stewardship — ultimately improving outcomes for New York’s aging and long-term care population.

title: Comprehensive KPI Tracking & Reporting Framework”
text:
The KPI tracking system is built on Google BigQuery as the central data warehouse. The architecture follows a four-layer pipeline model: Ingestion → Storage → Transformation → Presentation.

Layer 1 — Ingestion: Raw data flows into BigQuery from OALTC-licensed program submissions, ITS-managed applications, Medicaid claims, MDS feeds, and survey system exports. Each data feed is assigned a schema, ingestion schedule, and validation ruleset.
Layer 2 — Raw Storage (Data Lake): Unprocessed source data is stored in partitioned BigQuery tables by program, date, and source system. All raw records are retained for auditability and reprocessing.
Layer 3 — Transformation (Data Mart): SQL-based ETL pipelines transform raw data into clean, analysis-ready tables. KPI calculations, denominator logic, and exclusion rules are encoded here using version-controlled SQL scripts or dbt models.
Layer 4 — Presentation: Transformed KPI tables power dashboards (Looker Studio or Tableau), automated reports, and self-service query interfaces for OALTC program staff.




Data quality is enforced at each pipeline stage using the following six-dimension framework:









Dimension
Definition
Validation Rule (Example)
Action if Failed


Completeness
All required fields are populated
Null rate < 2% for facility_id, report_date, and outcome fields
Flag record; alert Data Steward; exclude from KPI calc until resolved


Validity
Values fall within defined ranges and formats
Readmission rate between 0–100%; date format = YYYY-MM-DD
Reject record; log error; notify submitter


Timeliness
Data arrives within the expected submission window
Monthly feeds ingested by the 10th of the following month
Trigger escalation alert; mark period as provisional


Consistency
Values are consistent across linked tables and time periods
Facility bed count in submissions matches licensed capacity in registry
Flag discrepancy; hold for reconciliation


Accuracy
Values reflect real-world program activity
Outlier detection: z-score > 3 triggers manual review
Queue for analyst review; annotate in dashboard


Uniqueness
No duplicate records in the analysis dataset
Composite key (facility_id + resident_id + event_date) must be unique
De-duplicate; log count of removed records






Each KPI is computed via a standardized SQL view in BigQuery. Below is the generalized template:




CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW oaltc_kpi.readmission_rate_monthly AS
SELECT
facility_id,
facility_name,
report_year,
report_month,
COUNT(CASE WHEN readmitted_30d = TRUE THEN 1 END) AS numerator,
COUNT(*) AS denominator,
ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNT(CASE WHEN readmitted_30d = TRUE THEN 1 END),
COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS readmission_rate_pct,
CASE
WHEN SAFE_DIVIDE(…) * 100 > 20 THEN ‘ALERT’
WHEN SAFE_DIVIDE(…) * 100 > 15 THEN ‘WARNING’
ELSE ‘ON TARGET’
END AS performance_status
FROM oaltc_raw.nh_discharge_events
WHERE data_quality_flag = ‘PASS’
AND discharge_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 13 MONTH)
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4;

While standard KPI tracking captures what has happened, the Bureau of Data Analytics and Automation can deliver significantly greater value by layering predictive and explanatory analytics on top of the core KPI framework. This transforms the system from a rearview mirror into an early-warning and decision-support tool.




Ensemble machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost) can be trained on historical KPI trends to predict which facilities are at elevated risk of deteriorating performance in the next 30–90 days — enabling proactive intervention before a deficiency occurs.
Time-series forecasting (ARIMA, Prophet, LSTM) can project KPI trajectories under different intervention scenarios, supporting resource allocation planning.
Risk stratification models can flag facilities for prioritized oversight based on a composite risk score combining multiple KPIs, complaint history, and staffing data.





SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values can identify which factors — staffing levels, ownership type, payer mix, geographic context — are the primary drivers of KPI variation across facilities.
Geographically Weighted models can reveal whether the relationship between staffing and outcomes differs by region, enabling targeted policy responses rather than one-size-fits-all interventions.





Stratified KPI analysis by race, ethnicity, payer type, and geography quantifies disparity gaps and tracks progress toward equity goals over time.
Spatial clustering analysis (Moran’s I, LISA) can identify geographic hotspots of poor performance, directing inspection and support resources to underserved areas.

title: Alert & Escalation System
text:
This section introduces an automated system designed to flag nursing home facilities that breach established KPI thresholds. The alert system provides structured escalation and clear response timelines based on the severity and persistence of performance issues:

Alert Detection: The system continuously monitors KPIs (such as 30-day readmission rate, staff turnover, and complaint investigation timeliness) for each facility. When a facility’s KPI exceeds (or falls below, if lower is better) specific thresholds, the system generates an alert.
Tiered Escalation Levels:

ALERT: Triggered when a facility breaches a KPI threshold for two or more consecutive periods (e.g., months or quarters). Assigns responsibility to the Bureau Chief or Program Director, requiring action within 2 days. Implies the need for urgent investigation and intervention.
WARNING: Triggered when a threshold is breached in the most recent period only. Assigns responsibility to the Program Manager, with a recommended response within 5 days. Indicates emerging risk.
ON TARGET: No action required; the facility is operating within target ranges.

Automated Assignments and Timelines: Each alert record specifies the required escalation level, the assigned responder, and the due date for follow-up, ensuring accountability and timely corrective action.

This proactive alerting and escalation framework aims to enable faster detection and resolution of quality, staffing, and compliance problems, supporting data-driven oversight and improving resident outcomes.


This section introduces the logic that automatically scans facility KPIs and determines whether any performance thresholds have been breached. Facilities that exceed risk limits—for example, if their 30-day readmission rate or staff turnover is too high, or their complaint investigation timeliness is too low—are flagged with an alert or warning based on the severity. The logic not only identifies which KPI was breached, but also assigns escalation levels (ALERT vs. WARNING), recommends which staff role should be responsible for follow-up, and sets a target due date for corrective action.
